database.what: Everything PostgreSQL will tell this service about itself, and the state of the schema this service owns in it.
persistence.why.notPostgres: persistence.mode is "{{mode}}", so this service has no database to report on. `memory` writes nothing at all and `ldif` writes RFC 2849 files — neither has a connection, a pool or a catalog. Set persistence.mode to `postgres` (it is restart-only: the store is opened before the listener binds).
persistence.why.noStore: persistence.mode is "postgres" and this process has NO OPEN STORE. That is a fault rather than a configuration: the store is opened from persistence.start() before the listener binds, and a failure there is fatal — so a running service in this state has had its store stopped underneath it. The startup log names what happened.
persistence.why.noMetrics: the open driver reports no metrics function, which means a build of persistence_postgres.js older than 2026-09-11.
persistence.status.coordinating: Processes against this store COORDINATE: every change is written to a monotonic log inside the transaction that made it, and each process applies what the others committed. The LISTEN/NOTIFY nudge only makes that prompt — the log is the contract, so a missed notification costs latency and never a change. What is NOT shared is sockets: the KDC, the LDAP listeners, the TLS ports and SPIFFE's four are per process, and the replay caches converge rather than synchronise. What this service MINTS — sessions, tokens, codes, artifacts, Kerberos tickets, the counters and the audit log — is persisted in PRODUCT mode on a postgres store, encrypted under the same key-encryption key as the signing keys, and in no other configuration: development mode regenerates the signing key on every start, so a restored token would verify against nothing.
persistence.status.notCoordinating: Persistence is not coordination in this configuration. Two processes pointed at one store each hold their own copy in memory and will not see each other's writes until they restart. Set persistence.coordinate on a postgres store to change that. What this service MINTS — sessions, tokens, codes, artifacts, Kerberos tickets, the counters and the audit log — is persisted in PRODUCT mode on a postgres store, encrypted under the same key-encryption key as the signing keys, and in no other configuration: development mode regenerates the signing key on every start, so a restored token would verify against nothing.
persistence.status.tlsVerified: TLS, sslmode={{sslmode}}; the server certificate is verified against this process's trust anchors.
persistence.status.tlsUnverified: TLS, sslmode={{sslmode}}; the server certificate is NOT verified (persistence.databaseTlsRejectUnauthorized is off), which is the honest setting for the self-signed pair the compose stack generates. The connection is encrypted either way.
persistence.status.tlsDefaultVerified: TLS — the connection string sets no sslmode, and this service dials every database over TLS; the server certificate is verified against this process's trust anchors.
persistence.status.tlsDefaultUnverified: TLS — the connection string sets no sslmode, and this service dials every database over TLS; the server certificate is NOT verified (persistence.databaseTlsRejectUnauthorized is off). The connection is encrypted either way.
persistence.status.tlsPreferVerified: TLS, sslmode=prefer — dialled over TLS only: libpq would fall back to a connection in the clear for prefer, and this service never does; the server certificate is verified against this process's trust anchors.
persistence.status.tlsPreferUnverified: TLS, sslmode=prefer — dialled over TLS only: libpq would fall back to a connection in the clear for prefer, and this service never does; the server certificate is NOT verified (persistence.databaseTlsRejectUnauthorized is off). The connection is encrypted either way.
persistence.status.tlsVerifyFull: TLS, sslmode=verify-full; the server certificate is verified against this process's trust anchors and its host name is checked, as the sslmode asks, whatever persistence.databaseTlsRejectUnauthorized says.
persistence.status.tlsVerifyCa: TLS, sslmode=verify-ca; the server certificate is verified against this process's trust anchors, as the sslmode asks, whatever persistence.databaseTlsRejectUnauthorized says — but its host name is NOT checked: verify-ca, as libpq reads it, trusts any certificate a trusted authority issued. Use verify-full to check the name as well.
persistence.status.refusedClear: NOT DIALLED — sslmode={{sslmode}} asks for a connection in the clear, which this service never opens, so it does not start on this connection string.
persistence.status.tlsUnknown: NOT DIALLED — the connection string is not a postgres:// URL, so whether it would be dialled in the clear cannot be told, and this service does not start on it.
persistence.status.notAUrl: the connection string is not a URL; nothing about it is shown, because it carries a password.
postgres.probes.server.what: Which PostgreSQL this is, who this service is connected AS, and how long the server has been up.
postgres.probes.size.what: How much disk this database occupies.
postgres.probes.database.what: Every counter PostgreSQL keeps for this database: commits and rollbacks, blocks read against blocks found in cache, tuples in every direction, deadlocks, temp files, and the I/O and session timings where the server collects them.
postgres.probes.conflicts.what: Queries cancelled by recovery conflicts. All zero on a server that is not a standby, which is the ordinary case here.
postgres.probes.connections.what: How many backends this database has, against the server's limit.
postgres.probes.backends.what: One row per backend on this database. A backend belonging to another role shows as a row with its state and its query withheld, which is what a non-monitoring role is shown.
postgres.probes.locks.what: Locks held and waited for, by mode. A waiting lock on a mock is almost always this service contending with itself across the request-worker pool.
postgres.probes.bgwriter.what: The background writer. ELEVEN columns before PostgreSQL 17 and FOUR from 17, when the checkpoint counters moved out of it — which is why this asks for all of them rather than naming any.
postgres.probes.checkpointer.what: The checkpointer. A view of its own since PostgreSQL 17; before that these counters are the tail of pg_stat_bgwriter above.
postgres.probes.wal.what: Write-ahead log generation. PostgreSQL 14 and later.
postgres.probes.archiver.what: WAL archiving. All zero unless archive_mode is on, which it is not in any stack this repository ships.
postgres.probes.replication.what: Standbys streaming from this server. EMPTY is the ordinary answer, and it is also what a role without pg_monitor is shown when there ARE standbys — so an empty table here is two different facts and the page says which one it cannot tell apart.
postgres.probes.tables.what: Every counter PostgreSQL keeps per table: sequential and index scans, tuples in every direction, live and dead rows, and when each was last vacuumed and analysed.
postgres.probes.tableIo.what: Per-table block I/O: how much came out of the buffer cache and how much off disk, for the heap, its indexes and its TOAST.
postgres.probes.sizes.what: How much disk each table occupies, split into the heap, its indexes and its TOAST, with the planner's row estimate.
postgres.probes.indexes.what: Every index, how often it has been scanned, how big it is, and whether it is a primary key or unique.
postgres.probes.columns.what: Every column of every table this service owns, with its type, whether it may be null, and its default.
postgres.probes.constraints.what: Primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys and checks.
postgres.probes.settings.what: Every setting an operator has changed from its built-in default, and where it was set — plus the handful that matter whether or not anybody touched them.
